props.title: L'Eclisse

sections.content: L'Eclisse (1962) represents Michelangelo Antonioni's masterful completion of his alienation trilogy, following L'Avventura (1960) and La Notte (1961). Monica Vitti delivers a haunting performance as Vittoria, wandering through Rome's EUR district - a modernist wasteland of concrete and steel. The film's revolutionary seven-minute ending, showing empty streets and unfinished buildings without any characters, influenced generations of filmmakers from Andrei Tarkovsky to Martin Scorsese. Antonioni strips away conventional plot to focus on architectural spaces and human disconnection. L'Avventura|1960|A woman vanishes during a yacht trip, but her friend and boyfriend become romantically involved while searching for her|Criterion Channel Red Desert|1964|Antonioni's first color film follows a neurotic woman struggling with industrial modernity|HBO Max Blow-Up|1966|A fashion photographer believes he's captured a murder on film in swinging London|TCM

The film's exploration of modern alienation directly influenced the French New Wave, particularly Last Year at Marienbad (1961) and 2 or 3 Things I Know About Her (1967). Antonioni's use of architecture as a character itself - with the EUR district's fascist-era buildings looming over the characters - created a template for how cinema could capture urban isolation. This approach echoes through later works like Playtime (1967) and The Passenger (1975). SUBHEAD: Visual Innovation and Lasting Impact

Antonioni's radical visual style in L'Eclisse broke new ground in cinema language. His use of empty frames, architectural compositions, and extended sequences without dialogue influenced directors like Edward Yang and Tsai Ming-liang. The famous ending sequence, where the film abandons its characters completely, reverberates through works like Jeanne Dielman, 23 Quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975) and Paris, Texas (1984), showing how physical spaces can carry emotional weight.
